records.why: The old text said the abnormal shape "prevents efficient oxygen transport". The real problem is blocked vessels and red cells that break down early; the shape itself comes from a changed haemoglobin gene. The same correction is made in Lesson 8 and in the Final Explanation. records.group_headline: Sickle-cell explanation corrected: a gene change alters haemoglobin, cells become stiff, block vessels and break down early (not simply "carry oxygen less well")
records.reference: WHO fact sheet "Sickle-cell disease"; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Erythrocytes (sickle-cell disease)
records.old: These children suffer painful crises because the abnormal shape prevents efficient oxygen transport. This phenomenon supports the concept that a tiny change in cell shape has dramatic consequences for function.
records.new: A change in one gene alters the haemoglobin protein, which makes the red blood cells curve and stiffen. These stiff cells block small blood vessels, causing painful crises, and break down early, causing anaemia. This phenomenon supports the concept that a tiny change in cell structure has dramatic consequences for function.

records.why: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning was defined wrongly in Lessons 2, 6, 9 and 10: "Evidence" was a scientist's idea or a concept rather than data or observations, and in Lesson 6 the "Claim" was what the learner observed. Guideline 7: Claim = the answer to the question; Evidence = data or observations; Reasoning = the science idea linking them. Each lesson now uses that definition, and Lesson 2 gets an example of a good answer for teachers.
records.group_headline: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning was defined wrongly in Lessons 2, 6, 9 and 10 (evidence was an idea, claim was an observation); now Claim = answer, Evidence = observation, Reasoning = science idea
records.old: Your CLAIM answers: How did Amina's body make new skin cells? Your EVIDENCE comes from Virchow's contribution. Your REASONING explains the mechanism.'
records.new: Your CLAIM is the answer: where did Amina's new skin cells come from? Your EVIDENCE is what we can observe: in the Lesson 1 photo sequence, new pink skin spreads in from the edges of the cut over a few days. Your REASONING is the science idea that links them: Virchow's tenet that all cells come from pre-existing cells.' WHAT A GOOD PARAGRAPH SOUNDS LIKE: 'The new skin cells came from skin cells that were already at the edge of the cut (Claim). In the photos, new pink skin spreads in from the edges over a few days (Evidence). Because every cell comes from a pre-existing cell, the new skin cells must have been made when existing skin cells divided (Reasoning).'

LIGHT vs ELECTRON MICROSCOPE (2 minutes; learners fill a two-row table, Light microscope | Electron microscope, from the card or textbook): 'Our school microscope uses light and glass lenses. It magnifies up to about ×400 here (about ×1000 at best) and can only show two points as separate if they are more than about 0.2 micrometres apart, so we see cells, the nucleus and the vacuole but not ribosomes. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons: it magnifies ×100 000 or more and separates points far closer together, so it shows ultrastructure such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes. records.old: Reasoning: the normal biconcave shape lets red blood cells carry oxygen to the tissues. records.new:
— Stage 1–2: Call Student A: 'Blood leaks out when the skin is cut. Which cells make the blood red, and what is their shape?' WAIT 12 seconds. EXPECTED: red blood cells, biconcave discs with no nucleus, packed with haemoglobin; they carry oxygen but do not stop the bleeding.
— Stage 3 (clot): Call Student B: 'Platelets come next. What is unusual about platelet structure, and how does that help them do their job?' WAIT 12 seconds. EXPECTED: platelets are tiny cell fragments with no nucleus; when activated they become sticky and spiky and release chemicals that start clotting, so they plug the cut.
— Stage 3 (clot continued): Call Student C: 'A clot is held together by a net of a protein called fibrin. Which organelle in cells makes proteins?' WAIT 10 seconds. EXPECTED: ribosomes (many of them on the rough endoplasmic reticulum).
— Stage 4 (immune): Call Student D: 'Neutrophils arrive. What do they do, and what organelle makes that job possible?' WAIT 12 seconds. EXPECTED: they engulf and digest bacteria; lysosomes full of digestive enzymes (and a flexible shape that lets them squeeze out of blood vessels).
— Stage 4 continued: Call Student E: 'Macrophages come later. How is their shape different from neutrophils, and what does it allow them to do?' WAIT 12 seconds. EXPECTED: larger, irregular and flexible; they engulf bacteria, dead cells and debris.
— Stage 5 (rebuilding): Call Student F: 'Fibroblasts secrete collagen. What organelle is highly developed in fibroblasts, and why is that logical?' WAIT 12 seconds. EXPECTED: rough endoplasmic reticulum (with the Golgi apparatus), because collagen is a protein that the cell makes and sends out.
— Stage 6 (skin closes): Call Student G: 'Epidermal cells divide and migrate. What must happen inside a cell before it can divide?' WAIT 10 seconds. EXPECTED: the nucleus copies its DNA (in animal cells the centrioles help separate the copies) and mitochondria supply the energy.
— SYNTHESIS: Call Student H: 'The cells of one body that have a nucleus all carry the same DNA. Platelets and mature red blood cells have lost theirs. So why do these cells look so different? Answer using what you know about specialisation.' WAIT 15 seconds — this is the hardest question. EXPECTED: different genes are switched on in different cells, so each cell makes the structures and proteins its job needs (accept 'each cell uses only the instructions it needs').

records.old: (b) Gene expression is selective, so cells with the same DNA end up with different structures. For example, the onion epidermal cells we observed had a cell wall, vacuole and nucleus but no chloroplasts, while a plant palisade cell has dense chloroplasts. This shows that a cell's structures follow the job it is specialised to do, not simply the DNA it carries.
